source_refs.note: Topic 18.8.1 with X-linked recessive, X-linked dominant and Y-linked traits and the SRY For Information box (PDF 106-108); Figures 18.15 to 18.17 are replaced by the original diagrams.

blocks.text: X-linked recessive traits are less common in females than in males. A female shows such a trait only when both her X chromosomes carry the recessive allele, while a male shows it with only one allele on his X, because the Y carries no allele of the gene. So the trait appears in every male who has its allele. Examples are muscular dystrophy, red-green colour-blindness and haemophilia.

items: If a mother has the trait, all her sons have it.
If a mother is a carrier (heterozygous), 50% of her sons can inherit it.
If a father has it, all his daughters are carriers, because they receive his X, and no son inherits it, because sons do not receive his X.

blocks.alt: Three family charts using circles for females and squares for males; filled shapes are affected and circles with a dot are carriers. Carrier mother XH Xh x normal father XH Y: one normal and one carrier daughter, one normal and one affected son. Normal mother x affected father Xh Y: both daughters carriers, both sons normal. Affected mother Xh Xh x normal father: daughters carriers, all sons affected.
blocks.caption: Inheritance of X-linked recessive traits (original diagram after Figure 18.15).
blocks.long_description: An X-linked recessive allele (h) shows in a male whenever he has it, because his only X comes from his mother and the Y carries no matching allele; a female shows it only if both her X chromosomes carry it. So a carrier mother passes it to half her sons, who are affected, and half her daughters, who are carriers; an affected father passes his X to every daughter, who become carriers, and to no son; an affected mother has all sons affected. Examples given in the book are haemophilia A and B, red-green colour-blindness and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

blocks.text: Examples given by the book are vitamin D-resistant rickets (inability to metabolize vitamin D properly, which softens and weakens the bones), Rett syndrome (a neuro-developmental disorder with loss of speech, repetitive hand movements and problems with walking) and Aicardi syndrome (abnormal development of the brain).

items: If the mother has the trait (homozygous or heterozygous), 50% of her children can inherit it; a homozygous mother passes it to all.
If the father has it, all his daughters inherit it and no son does.

blocks.title: Equal in both sexes?
blocks.text: The book says X-linked dominant traits are in equal ratio in females and males. Because a female has two X chromosomes and so two chances to carry the allele, these traits are usually about twice as common in females.

blocks.alt: Three family charts. X-linked dominant, affected mother XD Xd x normal father: one affected and one normal child of each sex. X-linked dominant, affected father XD Y x normal mother: both daughters affected, both sons normal. Y-linked, affected father carrying allele t on his Y: every son affected, every daughter normal. A notes panel lists the book's examples.
blocks.caption: X-linked dominant and Y-linked inheritance (original diagram after Figures 18.16 and 18.17).
blocks.long_description: An X-linked dominant allele (D) shows whenever it is present, in either sex. A heterozygous affected mother passes it to half of her children, sons or daughters; an affected father passes his X to every daughter, so all daughters are affected, and no son is. The book's examples are vitamin D-resistant rickets, Rett syndrome and Aicardi syndrome. Y-linked (holandric) genes lie on the part of the Y that has no matching region on the X, so they appear only in males and pass from father to every son; the book's examples are hypertrichosis of the ear rim, 'porcupine man' and webbed toes.

blocks.text: The Y chromosome has relatively few genes compared with the X, so Y-linked traits are rare. Y-linked genes have no alleles on the X; they are called holandric genes and lie only on the non-homologous region of the Y. Y-linked traits appear only in males and pass from father to son only. The book's examples are hypertrichosis (hair on the rim of the pinna), 'porcupine man' (straight hair on the body) and webbing of the toes; the genetic basis of these examples is debated.

blocks.title: For information: the SRY gene
blocks.text: Human males have a specific gene on the Y chromosome called SRY (sex-determining region Y). It makes a protein that starts the development of the testes and prevents the development of female reproductive structures.

blocks.prompt: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is not a carrier. What are the chances for their sons and daughters?
blocks.explanation: Sons get their mother's normal X, so none is colour-blind; every daughter gets the father's X, so all daughters are carriers with normal vision.

items: X-linked recessive: commoner in males; carrier mother passes to half her sons.
X-linked dominant: affected father gives it to all daughters, no sons.
Y-linked (holandric): father to every son only; SRY starts testis development.
